Salesforce Inc (NYSE:CRM, XETRA:FOO) remains rated "buy" at Bank of America, which sees a favorable short-term outlook for the stock after a roughly 27% decline from its September peak.

The comapny is set to report its fiscal 2027 third-quarter results on December 2, and the bank is looking for signs of faster organic growth in the second half, momentum in cRPO and bookings, and stronger Agentforce monetization.

Bank of America projects Salesforce's organic revenue growth will rise to 7.4% in the third quarter and 9.9% in the fourth, from 6.4% in the second.

Warren Buffett and dividends are an old love story that continues to this day, as Berkshire's latest 13F filing shows. The filing also reveals portfolio changes as CEO Greg Abel reshapes Berkshire's stock holdings after succeeding Buffett in January as the Omaha, Nebraska-based conglomerate's leader. Berkshire bought $2.37 billion worth of stocks in the third quarter and sold $2.79 billion. You can read about the fund's latest holdings here.

Dividend stocks continued to take center stage in the portfolio. Most of Berkshire's holdings are in companies that pay dividends, and many of them offer solid payouts. This has been an important part of Buffett's investment strategy over the years, and his successors at the firm appear to share that approach.

Analysts have long questioned why Berkshire Hathaway does not pay dividends to its own shareholders. Buffett has always been confident in his ability to put the company's capital to better use. He believes investing in businesses and other opportunities can generate better returns than distributing cash to shareholders. Even when he feels Berkshire cannot find attractive investment opportunities for its growing cash pile, he would rather return capital through share buybacks than dividends. In a 2018 interview with CNBC, Buffett explained his thinking: "Dividends have the implied promise that you keep paying them forever and not decrease them." He has also argued that repurchasing Berkshire's own shares can be more beneficial for shareholders.

Also read: 10 Best Tech Stocks That Pay Dividends

In a 2023 report, The Wall Street Journal cited Todd Finkle, a professor of entrepreneurship at Gonzaga University and author of a book about Buffett's career. Finkle summed up Buffett's approach by saying, "That's what he loves: dividends and buybacks."

Finkle noted that Buffett has been particularly good at identifying businesses that can withstand different economic cycles while continuing to increase their dividends. These investments have helped grow the value of Berkshire's stock portfolio over time while bringing in cash that the company can use to support its businesses, make acquisitions, and buy back its own shares. For Buffett, dividends aren't "the secret sauce, but they're part of it," Finkle said. Given this backdrop, we will take a look at how much in estimated dividends Berkshire is expected to receive this year from some of its biggest holdings. Hartnett said a true bust could trigger a bear market and pull the S&P 500 down to about 6,666, or roughly 8% below current levels. Consensus global earnings growth forecasts of 15% to 20% may prove too optimistic as AI spending and wealth effects fade.

CEO Fermi Wang blamed rising memory prices and supply scarcity, which are prompting customers to lower forecasts, delay shipments, and cancel orders.

Bank of America downgraded Ambarella to 'Underperform' from 'Neutral', and slashed its price target to $30 from $70.

Morgan Stanley downgraded Ambarella to 'Equal Weight' from 'Overweight' and cut its price target to $42 from $70.

Ambarella (AMBA) shares fell to an 8-year low in morning trade on Wednesday after the chip designer forecast a steep drop in revenue and analysts cut price targets and downgraded the stock.

Ambarella forecast fourth-quarter (Q4) revenue of $70 million to $75 million, roughly 37% below the $115.2 million it reported in the prior quarter and about 35% below Wall Street expectations, according to Stifel. The firm cut its price target on Ambarella to $50 from $80 while maintaining a 'Buy' rating, according to TheFly.

Meanwhile, Bank of America (BofA) downgraded the shares to 'Underperform' from 'Neutral', and Morgan Stanley downgraded them to 'Equal Weight' from 'Overweight'.

CWeHm-wall-street-cuts-price-target-on-ambarella-after-q4-earnings-.png

AMBA stock hit lows last seen in November 2018 in morning trade, before paring losses.

Ambarella CEO Blames Rise In Memory Prices, Supply Crunch

Ambarella makes chips that process video and run AI applications in devices such as security cameras, dashcams and automobiles. However, rising memory prices and limited availability are forcing customers to scale back purchases, delay shipments or cancel orders, creating a near-term setback for Ambarella's growth outlook.

CEO Fermi Wang blamed "the unprecedented rise in memory prices and the scarcity of memory supply," stating that the pressure has intensified and prompted many customers to lower their forecasts.

According to Susquehanna, the pullback in consumer Internet of Things (IoT) shipments has been dramatic, with memory shortages prompting customers to cancel, delay or push out orders.

AI Boom Tightens Memory Supply

In its downgrade, Bank of America said "memory allocation uncertainty and strong AI memory demand" make it difficult to underwrite a near-term growth rebound. The firm cut its price target to $30 from $70 and lowered its fiscal 2028 pro forma earnings estimate to $0.12 per share from $1 per share.

Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley cut its price target to $42 from $70. The firm said it remains positive on Ambarella's technology but said its automotive business is taking longer to develop than expected, while its partner channel will need years to scale. It added that neither is likely to offset the near-term impact of the memory shortage.

title: Bank Bond Losses Hit $486 Billion: How Exposed Is Bank of America?
detail:
Bank Bond Losses Hit $486 Billion: How Exposed Is Bank of America?
Nikita Kataruka

WFC

Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Bank of America BAC faces mounting pressure on its securities portfolio as elevated interest rates weigh on bond valuations. According to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's Nov. 24 report, unrealized securities losses across U.S. banks surged 48.8% sequentially to $486 billion in the third quarter of 2026, highlighting persistent balance-sheet challenges.

BAC remains particularly exposed, given its substantial held-to-maturity ("HTM") securities portfolio, accumulated largely during the low-interest-rate environment. Its gross unrealized HTM securities losses increased 29.4% to $103.9 billion as of Sept. 30, 2026, from $80.3 billion at 2025-end. Although these losses do not directly affect earnings, they reflect significant deterioration in the market value of its investments.

Bank of America's exposure to longer-duration, lower-yielding securities limits its ability to capitalize on elevated interest rates. Selling these securities to reinvest proceeds at higher yields could crystallize losses, potentially hurting earnings and capital. Moreover, higher deposit costs alongside relatively low returns on legacy securities could restrict net interest margin expansion and weigh on profitability.

The substantial unrealized losses also reduce BAC's balance-sheet flexibility, particularly if unexpected liquidity needs arise. BAC's average global liquidity sources declined to $914 billion in the third quarter of 2026 from $975 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025. Nonetheless, its diversified deposit franchise, strong earnings generation and recurring securities cash flows mitigate the risk of forced asset sales.

Going forward, the gradual maturity of legacy securities should allow Bank of America to redeploy funds into potentially higher-yielding assets, supporting net interest income growth. While declining long-term yields could ease valuation pressures, persistently elevated rates may prolong balance-sheet constraints. Hence, disciplined portfolio repositioning, effective funding cost management and adequate liquidity will remain critical to BAC's profitability and financial flexibility.

How Do Bank of America's Peers Fare?

JPMorgan Chase JPM also faces securities valuation pressures stemming from elevated interest rates. As of Sept. 30, 2026, JPMorgan's HTM securities portfolio stood at $274.6 billion, up from $270.1 billion at 2025-end. Its available-for-sale ("AFS") securities portfolio increased to $547.2 billion.

However, JPMorgan's strong liquidity position provides considerable flexibility in managing interest rate risks. At the third-quarter end, JPM had approximately $1.5 trillion in liquidity sources, while its average deposits increased 8% year over year. Its diversified revenue streams and robust funding base should help mitigate the impact of securities valuation pressures.

Wells Fargo & Company WFC has been gradually reshaping its investment portfolio. At third-quarter end, Wells Fargo's HTM securities declined 10% year over year to $189.3 billion, while AFS securities increased 25% to $247.7 billion. Nonetheless, combined net unrealized losses on these portfolios increased from the figure at 2025-end, primarily reflecting interest rate movements.

Wells Fargo's declining HTM securities exposure and growing AFS portfolio could provide greater flexibility in balance-sheet management. However, persistent securities valuation pressures and potential increases in funding costs could temper the benefits of portfolio repositioning on NII growth.

title: Costco Hasn't Split Its Stock Since 2000. Here's Why 2027 Could Be the Year.
detail:
Costco Hasn't Split Its Stock Since 2000. Here's Why 2027 Could Be the Year.
Neil Patel, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 11:20 PM CST 5 min read
COST
NVDA
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Forward stock splits receive a lot of attention from investors. It might be because this move reminds shareholders how well the business has performed in the past. And it's a signal of confidence from the management team that executives are optimistic about the future. Investor psychology gets a boost.

If we focus just on the fundamentals, nothing really changes. Operations resume as normal. The same employees sell the same products and services to the same customers. It's business as usual.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The data is still worth highlighting. According to Bank of America and Bloomberg, companies that undergo a forward stock split see their share prices rise an average of 25% over the subsequent 12 months. Naturally, investors try to figure out who the next big candidates are, so they can potentially capture sizable gains in their portfolios.

This brings up Costco (NASDAQ:COST). It hasn't split its stock since 2000, but it could take action next year. Here's why.

Image source: Getty Images.

Why 2027 could look a lot like 2000

Costco's board of directors approved a 2-for-1 split on Dec. 2, 1999. It took effect on Jan. 14, 2000, turning a roughly $98 stock into a $49 one.

The business was performing well. Net revenue jumped 16% year over year in Q1 2020, and net income totaled $129.3 million.

Shares were pricey, too. The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio hit 44.3 at the start of 2000. In that era, split-adjusted prices were the standard way to keep an expensive stock within reach of everyday investors.

Fast-forward to today. Costco closed at $1,097.91 on Nov. 23, more than 11 times the price that triggered the last split. In fiscal 2026 (ended Aug. 30), net sales rose 10.1% to $297.2 billion, and diluted earnings per share (EPS) climbed 14% to $20.76. The trailing P/E is near 53.

Record share price. Healthy growth. A premium valuation. Today's setup rhymes with 2000.

Rival Walmart also split 3-for-1 in February 2024. This was partly to help employees buy shares.

But management hasn't tipped its hand. On the fiscal 2025 first-quarter call in December 2024, chief financial officer Gary Millerchip said, "There isn't a plan at this time for a stock split." He pointed to fractional-share trading, but said Costco would keep evaluating the idea.

Executives are clearly confident in the company's position. On Nov. 10, the board declared a $30 per-share special dividend worth $13.3 billion. With the share price above $1,000, however, the split question probably won't go away in 2027.

title: 4 Reasons to Roll Over Your 401(k) Into an IRA (And 4 Reasons Not To)

4 Reasons to Roll Over Your 401(k) Into an IRA (And 4 Reasons Not To)

Credit: Alamy

When you leave a job and walk out the door for the last time, you might pack up your photos, the spare pair of dress shoes stashed under your desk, your "I Love My Corgi" coffee mug and all your other personal items.

But what do you do with your 401(k) plan?

Most people roll the money over to an IRA because they gain access to more investment options and have more control over the account. Some brokerage firms sweeten the deal with cash incentives.

For example, Charles Schwab offers competitive incentives for 401(k) rollovers and IRA transfers, often through referral programs or targeted promotions where you can get up to $1,000, depending on the deposit amount and eligibility. Citi Personal Wealth Management and Merrill Edge, a Bank of America company, also offer incentives for 401(k) rollovers and IRA transfers.

Plus, moving your money to an IRA could help you streamline your investments and grow your wealth. Amy Thomas, a 43-year-old clinical trial coordinator in Lakewood, Colo., has rolled over 401(k) plans from three former employers into one place, which "makes everything a lot easier," she says. Now she doesn't worry that she'll lose track of an account that might have been left behind.

Move it, leave it alone or take a lump sum?
Credit: Getty Images

But a rollover isn't always the right move, and sometimes it's best to leave your money where it is. With millions of dollars to invest, large 401(k) plans have access to institutional-class funds that charge lower fees than their retail counterparts.

That means you could end up paying less to invest in the 401(k). That said, there are other perils to a rollover: If you're not careful, you could end up with a portfolio of high-cost investments with subpar returns.

What about cashing out the account when you leave your job and take a lump sum? Unless your financial situation is dire, that's never a good idea. You'll owe taxes on the entire amount in the year you receive it, plus a 10% early-withdrawal penalty if you're younger than 59-½.

Reasons to roll over
Credit: Getty Images

Rolling over the money from your 401(k) to an IRA is still the best move in many cases.

1. Your plan has high-cost investments.

Many large 401(k) plans offer low-cost options that have been carefully vetted by the plan's administrators, but other 401(k)s are hobbled by underperforming funds and high costs. And even low-cost plans may charge former employees higher administrative fees if they choose to keep their 401(k)s.

(Bloomberg) -- Trend-chasing quant funds are trimming their long-held short positions in US Treasuries, fueling a bond rally as an equity selloff revives haven demand for government debt.

Most Read from Bloomberg

China Sentences Official to Death for Spying for Foreign Power

Nvidia Board Reinstated CEO Without Consulting Management

Nasdaq 100 Sinks as AI Rout Fuels Gains in Bonds: Markets Wrap

Stocks Jump Most Since April 2025 as Huang Is Back: Markets Wrap

Commodity trading advisers — which seek to profit from momentum across asset classes — have reduced their Treasury shorts to about half their September peak, a Bank of America Corp. model shows. The $5 billion iMGP DBi Managed Futures Strategy exchange-traded fund, which aims to replicate trend-following strategies, cut its short duration exposure — a measure of interest-rate risk — to about negative 6.4 years as of Monday, from negative 7.1 years a week earlier.

CTAs, an investment cohort estimated to manage more than $400 billion, have been consistently betting against Treasuries this year as an oil-price spike, elevated inflation and the artificial-intelligence boom pushed 10-year yields to about 5.36% in October — the highest in more than two decades.

Since then, a swift unwind of the AI trade in stocks has clouded the growth outlook, pushing the 10-year yield down to about 4.9% and prompting trend followers to reduce short wagers. The group is still pessimistic overall with the Federal Reserve expected to raise interest rates again as soon as next month.

While the bearish trend in bonds remains intact, "it's a little bit choppier now than it was earlier this year," said Andrew Beer, founder of Dynamic Beta Investments, which manages the iMGP ETF.

The fund returned more than 17% this year through October, with much of the gain coming from long oil positions. Short Treasuries wagers were profitable until October, when the bond rally cost the position more than 3 percentage points and reduced its contribution to this year's return to about 1 percentage point. The ETF is now up about 14% this year through Monday.

Despite the setback, Beer said CTAs still have a "meaningful" bet on rising interest rates, reflecting concerns about sticky inflation and persistent fiscal deficits.

But it may not take much for the remaining bearish positions to unravel. Bank of America's model shows a roughly 20- to 25-basis-point drop in yields across the curve "would likely unwind most of the remaining shorts," said Chintan Kotecha, a derivatives analyst at the bank.
